chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Saeed al-A'raj, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) prayed, then gave the salām in two rak'at. So one behind him asked him, 'O Messenger of Allah! Did something new occur in the prayer?' He said: 'And what is that?' They said, 'You only prayed two rak'at.' So he said: 'Was it like that, O Zal al-Yadayn?' And he used to be called Zal al-Shimalayn. So he said: 'Yes'. So he built upon his prayer and completed the prayer with four (rak'at).

And he (peace be upon him) said: Indeed, Allah is the One who caused him to forget as a mercy for the community. Do you not see that if a man were to do this, he would be faulted and it would be said, 'Your prayer is not accepted'? So whoever enters upon him today, that one says, 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) established a Sunnah and it became an example, and he performed two prostrations for the sake of the speech.'

key_terms.ذَا الْيَدَيْنِ: Zal al-Yadayn (The Possessor of the Two Hands, a title for the Prophet)
key_terms.سَلَّمَ: gave the salām (concluding greeting of prayer)
key_terms.لِمَكَانِ الْكَلَامِ: for the sake of the speech/interruption

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on speaking during prayer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi records the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) pausing his prayer to converse with Mu'adh ibn Jabal, resulting in a shortened two-rak'ah prayer that he later completed to four. The narration highlights the principle of 'Nasi'ah' (divine forgetfulness) as a mercy to the Ummah, establishing that speaking during prayer does not invalidate it but requires completing the missed portion. This incident serves as a foundational legal precedent in Shia jurisprudence for the validity of Salāt despite minor interruptions or speech.
